nodes.text: Equal is the madness of those who, report tells, in dedicated
shrines consecrated Fever and Scabies as goddesses.
God is not the inventor of vice: an angel,
fallen from his kind, created it, conceived in his infamous mind,
he who once shone as an august star and, a vast
splendour made from nothing, blazed with the honour bestowed on him.
For all things of old are from nothing, and whatever anywhere has been made;
but not from nothing are God and the true Wisdom
and the Holy Spirit, a being ever living and never
begun, which also fashioned the airy ministers.
Of their number one, most beautiful of face,
proud in his majesty, while, increased with excessive strength,
he is puffed up, while, swelling hugely, he lifts himself higher
and displays his fires more boastfully than is allowed,
persuaded [himself] that, begotten by his own powers, he had from himself
taken for himself the matter by which he might first begin
to be, and that his birth had begun without an originator.
From this a school plans to beget a secretive sect,
which teaches that out of darkness a tyrant suddenly flashed forth,
who, as if lurking beneath eternal night, in times gone by
had lived, and had always reigned in a hidden age.
A rival, so they tell, to spoil the divine works, suddenly
he thrust his head out of the black murk.
But our reason denies this, which may not weaken the one
faith that was handed down in the sacred book.
‘Nothing,’ it says, ‘was made without God, but all things through him,
all things; nor is there anyone else except one made by him.’
But he, made good from the root, for the practice of goodness
brought forth, and serene from the first source of his kind,
soon grew worse of his own accord, when dark
envy stained him and goaded him with bitter spurs.
For a spark of hatred blazed up from the tinder of jealousy,
and sudden resentment fanned a wicked temper.
He had seen that the clay, an image and a built thing, by the breath
of God had grown warm, and that as lord over creation it was also
set, so that the nature of land and sea and sky,
serving man, should know how to pour forth a rich yield
and to make over what it poured forth to the earthly king.
With the fretting leaven of his mind he puffed up his swelling,
the beast, and, harsh, drew strength from his sour marrow;
the beast without filth, in whom upright wisdom then kept the youth
of his long body free of knots.
Behold, he folds new coils in his winding breast,
wrapping his gleaming belly in twisting spirals.
The tongue, once single, flickers with a varied art of speaking,
and, split by deceits, resounds with three-forked speech.
Hence the native source of the vices; from that prince
flowed the origin of evil, who first [learned] to corrupt himself,
